extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in medieval Italian political history
extracted.subtask_description: Narrative account of Siena's political conflicts, magistracies, militia laws, and civil wars in the late 13th–early 14th centuries, explaining causes and consequences of factional governance. Aimed at readers studying medieval Tuscan political history or comparative government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolization of government by a prevalent faction
rubrics_metrics.description: “This is ever the object of a prevalent faction, or a decided majority, to monopolize the whole government to themselves, by the total exclusion of the minority.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial explanation and examples: when a ruling faction concentrates legislative, executive and judicial power it drives opponents into exile, confiscates property, executes, and oppresses without control; such monopolization breeds resentment and continual instability (illustrated by Guelph actions against Ghibellines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of magistrates and exclusion of nobles as a tyrannical device
rubrics_metrics.description: The reduction of magistrates (thirty-six to fifteen, then to nine) and the ordinance that 'no gentleman could be of the number of fifteen, but all must be popular men' is described as 'tyrannical' and absurd, excluding descent or public service as merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: these numeric reductions and explicit exclusions (nobles rendered incapable of office) were defended as securing the state but are criticized as arbitrary, producing division, weakening the city, provoking the nobles, and failing to quiet factions; anti-pattern: excluding groups by birth rather than assessing fitness for office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of government in few hands can increase safety and durability
rubrics_metrics.description: “Perhaps it is universally true, that if the whole government must reside in a single assembly, it is more safe, peaceful, and durable, in a few hands than in many, an aristocracy than a democracy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's analytic claim: while such concentration may be injurious and oppressive to many, it can also make a government more stable and longer-lasting compared with broad participation when all power is vested in one centre; presented as a possible explanation for why restricted regimes sometimes endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of militia and public arms under pretense but for party security
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders that 300 men should always stand in arms in each third of the city, companies of forty-two with captains and gonfaloniers, chains across streets, and other military arrangements were instituted 'to prevent disorders' but in practice armed the popular party to secure themselves against the nobles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/anti-pattern: these public military measures, though presented as for public order, were instrumentalized by the governing faction to entrench power and preempt noble returns to authority; examples include standing guards, public ensigns, and laws excluding nobles from militia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of public defensive institutions into weapons of civil war
rubrics_metrics.description: Public arms and standing guards 'which had been provided by their ancestors for the conservation of their country and their liberties, were now most insolently converted into the weapons of civil war, and turned by the cunning of one party against the rights of another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: institutions intended for collective defence can be co-opted by factions and used to oppress rivals; warning that such repurposing deepens civil strife and undermines the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal disqualification ('making grandees') to permanently exclude families from office
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of formally admonishing or declaring certain families 'grandees'—rendering them incapable of serving in the supreme magistracy—so that 'ninety families were admonished ... rendered incapable of the magistracy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: this legal mechanism was used to cement oligarchic control by permanently excluding rivals; consequence: concentration of wealth and power, resentment, and continued conflict as excluded families retained allies and resources to contest rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social stratification and factional alliances as drivers of instability
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions among nobles, the popolo minuto (lower classes), the popolo grasso (wealthier commoners/merchants), and merchants produced shifting alliances (e.g., plebeians joining nobles against merchant government), leading to riots, sieges, and repeated civil wars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: the natural distrust among social orders (nobility vs commons, popolo minuto vs popolo grasso) creates opportunities for factional coalitions and rebellions; examples include unions of plebeians with nobles against merchant oligarchs and the recurring armed conflicts that followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private hatreds among noble families escalate into public ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: Private enmities and hereditary hatreds among noble houses (e.g., Tolomei and Salimbeni) repeatedly precipitated tumults, street battles, and wider civil disturbance that imperilled the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: rulers attempting to restrain these disputes by decrees or by reducing numbers of magistrates often failed; the author treats such private rivalries as an important cause of broader political breakdown and as a justification (or pretext) for government reforms that sometimes backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace and reconciliation as remedies for factional danger
rubrics_metrics.description: When popular indignation and fear of internal collapse arose, the pope's legate recommended reconciliation: 'it appeared to them, that for the common tranquillity, a peace ought to be concluded,' and in 1279 exiles were restored 'to the universal satisfaction of all parties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: negotiated reconciliation and restoration of exiles are presented as effective means to restore public tranquillity in the short term; example: the 1279 peace mediated by the legate ended some hostilities and allowed exiles to return under a signory.
